transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess the main thing that finally made me come in is my eating. It’s been all turned around for months now, and I don’t really know what to make of it. Some days I barely want anything—I’ll just sort of pick at a piece of toast and drink coffee and then realize that’s mostly all I’ve had. And then other days I’ll be standing in the bakery aisle buying sweets, like pastries or cookies, things I don’t even really enjoy once I get them home. It feels strange, like I’m not eating in any normal way anymore.
Have you lost any weight over these months?

I’m not completely sure about the number, honestly. I haven’t been keeping track on a scale like I probably should. It’s more that my eating has been so… uneven. Like I said, some days I’ll hardly eat anything, just toast and coffee, and then I realize the whole day’s gone by like that. And then other days I’m buying sweets in the bakery aisle—cookies, pastries, things like that—even though when I get home I don’t really want them or enjoy them.

So I don’t know if I’ve lost weight exactly, but my appetite and the way I eat have definitely changed for months now. It doesn’t feel normal for me.
Do you ever think about your weight or body shape when you're deciding what or how much to eat?

No, I don’t think it’s really about my weight or how I look. I mean, I’m not standing there thinking, “I should eat less because of my body,” or anything like that. It’s more like… I just don’t feel interested in food some days, or I forget, or nothing sounds worth making. And then other times I’ll buy sweet things almost automatically, but not because I’m trying to change my shape or because I’m worried about calories. It feels more scattered than that.
Do you ever feel guilty after eating?

Guilty after eating… I don’t know. Not in the way I think you mean, like because I ate too much or because of my weight or anything. I don’t really sit there counting it up afterward or feeling like I’ve done something wrong because I had food.

Sometimes I feel kind of bad or embarrassed when I notice how odd it’s gotten—like if I bought a bunch of sweets and then they’re just sitting there and I barely even want them. Then I think, “Why did I do that?” But it’s more confusion than guilt, I guess. And on the days I hardly eat, I don’t really feel proud or guilty either. It’s just like… the day disappears and then I realize I didn’t take care of myself very well.
Do you ever worry about gaining weight?

No, I don’t really worry about gaining weight. That’s not what’s in my head when I’m eating or not eating.

It’s more that my eating has gotten all turned around for months now, and that’s actually part of why I came in. Some days I just sort of pick at toast and coffee and don’t have any real interest in anything else, and then other days I’ll find myself standing in the bakery aisle buying cookies or pastries or whatever sweet thing is there, even though I don’t really enjoy it when I get home. It’s not because I’m scared of gaining weight or trying to control my body. It just feels… off, like I’m not eating in a normal way for me anymore.
Do you notice that your eating habits change in response to how you're feeling emotionally?

Yes, I think so, though it’s not always clear to me in the moment. It’s more like my eating follows whatever state I’m in without me deciding it. When I’m feeling really low or shut down, food just sort of drops away. I’ll have toast and coffee, maybe pick at something, and then suddenly it’s late and I realize I never made a real meal.

And then other times, when I feel unsettled or empty or just… I don’t know, not right, I’ll end up in the bakery aisle buying sweets. Cookies, pastries, things like that. It’s almost automatic, like I’m trying to fix something, but then I get home and I don’t even really enjoy them. They just sit there, or I eat some and it doesn’t do much.

That’s part of why I came in, honestly. It’s been going on for months, this back and forth where some days I barely eat and other days I’m buying sweet things I don’t even want. It doesn’t feel normal for me.
Do you think your eating habits are affected by stress?

Yes… I think stress probably does affect it, though it’s hard for me to separate stress from just feeling low or off, because it all kind of runs together lately.

What I notice is that my eating has been really turned around for months now. Some days, if I’m tense or overwhelmed, I don’t really eat properly at all. I’ll just have toast and coffee and sort of pick at it, and then I realize hours later that I never made an actual meal. It doesn’t feel like a choice exactly—it’s more like food just becomes too much effort, or I don’t have any interest in it.

Then other days, especially when I feel unsettled, I’ll end up in the bakery aisle buying sweets—cookies or pastries or things like that. And in the moment it feels like I’m doing something, like maybe it’ll help somehow, but then I get home and I don’t even really enjoy them. Sometimes they just sit there, or I eat a little and it doesn’t feel like anything.

So yes, I’d say stress is mixed up in it. It’s one of the reasons I came in, because this isn’t how I normally eat, and it’s been going on long enough that I’m worried about it.
Are there any areas of your life, such as work, relationships, or daily activities, that you feel are being affected by your current eating habits?

Yes… it has, more than I wanted to admit at first. I still get through the basic things for my aunt — I make sure she’s taken care of, and I don’t just abandon what has to be done — but it all feels so much harder than it used to.

It’s like, if I haven’t eaten right or I’ve just had coffee and toast and then nothing, I don’t have the steadiness for the rest of the day. And then on the days where I’ve bought sweets and feel bad or just kind of weighed down by it, I don’t really feel any better either. So things pile up.

I’ve missed church planning calls, which I normally would not do. I’ve put off some fair projects I said I’d help with. And there are things around town or with my aunt where I’ve had to ask neighbors to cover for me, things I used to just handle without making a big deal out of it. That’s embarrassing, honestly, because I’ve always tried to be dependable.

So yes, I’d say it’s affecting caregiving and just staying involved in town. I’m still doing the basics, but it feels like I’m dragging myself through them, and I’m not keeping up the way I used to.
Do you feel like eating or buying food is a way for you to cope with difficult emotions?

Yes… I think it is, at least sometimes. Not in a way that feels very deliberate, though. It’s not like I say to myself, “I’m upset, so I’m going to buy food.” It’s more like I’m already feeling bad or empty or restless, and then I find myself standing in the bakery aisle looking at sweets, and I’ve already put cookies or pastries in the basket before I’ve really thought it through.

That’s part of why I came in, because my eating has gotten all turned around for months now. Some days I barely want anything and I’m just picking at toast and coffee, and then other days I’m buying sweet things I don’t even really enjoy once I get them home. It feels like I’m trying to do something to make myself feel better, but it doesn’t actually work. It just makes me feel strange about myself afterward, like I don’t understand why I did it.
Do you think that when you buy or eat sweets, you're trying to improve your mood?

Yes… I think that’s probably what’s happening, or at least part of what’s happening. It doesn’t feel very clear in the moment, like I’m not standing there thinking, “This will fix my mood.” But I do think I’m trying to feel something different, maybe just for a minute.

That’s really why I came in, because my eating has gotten so turned around for months now. Some days I’m barely eating, just sort of picking at toast and coffee and not making a real meal, and then other days I end up standing in the bakery aisle buying sweets. Cookies, pastries, whatever looks like it might be comforting, I guess. But then I get them home and I don’t even really enjoy them. It’s like I thought it would help, but it doesn’t land the way I expected.

So yes, I think maybe I’m trying to improve my mood, but it doesn’t really work. It just leaves me feeling more confused about why I did it.
Do you ever feel like you're losing control when you're eating?

Yes… sometimes it does feel that way, though maybe not like I’m sitting there eating and can’t physically stop. It’s more the whole thing leading up to it feels out of my hands.

I mean, that’s part of why I came in. My eating has just gotten so turned around these past months. Some days I’ll hardly eat anything proper — just coffee and a piece of toast, maybe picking at something later but not making a real meal. And then another day I’ll find myself in the bakery aisle, buying sweets like cookies or pastries, and it feels like I’ve already done it before I’ve really decided to.

Then when I get home, I don’t even enjoy them much. I’ll look at what I bought and think, “Why did I do that?” So yes, in that sense, it feels like I’m not quite in control of it. Not every single time, but enough that it bothers me.
Do you notice your eating habits changing when you're feeling sad or anxious?

Yes, I do think it changes with how I’m feeling. It’s not always neat enough that I can say, “I felt sad at noon, then I ate this at one,” but when I’m low or wound up inside, my eating gets… strange. It’s like I lose the normal rhythm of it.

That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because for months now it’s been all turned around. Some days I don’t want much of anything, and I’ll just pick at toast and drink coffee, and then I realize the whole day has gone by and I haven’t really eaten a proper meal. And other days, especially when I feel empty or unsettled, I’ll end up in the bakery aisle buying sweets — cookies or pastries — like they’re going to help somehow.

But then I get them home and I don’t even really enjoy them. Sometimes I just look at them and feel worse, like I don’t understand what I was trying to do. So yes… when I’m sad or anxious, my eating definitely seems to shift, but not in a way that feels healthy or satisfying.
Are there people in your life who have noticed a change in your eating habits or overall well-being?

Yes… I think so. I mean, nobody has sat me down exactly and said, “Your eating habits have changed,” but I think people can tell something is off. It’s hard not to notice, I guess, because it’s been going on for months now.

That’s really one of the reasons I came in. My eating feels like it’s gotten completely turned around. Some days I’ll just have coffee and maybe pick at toast, and I’ll sort of tell myself I’ll eat something proper later, but then later doesn’t really happen. And then other days I do the opposite thing, where I end up in the bakery aisle buying sweets — cookies, pastries, things like that — even though when I get them home I don’t really enjoy them the way I thought I would.

So I think people around me probably notice that I’m not eating normally, or that I don’t seem like myself overall. I try not to make a big display of it, but it’s been hard to hide because it’s become such a strange pattern.
Do you feel like you're eating in response to feeling like you might lose control of your emotions?

Yes… I think that’s close to it. I don’t know if I’d say I’m thinking, “I’m going to lose control of my emotions, so I should eat,” not that clearly. It’s more muddled than that. But when I feel like I’m getting overwhelmed inside, my eating is one of the first things that seems to go off track.

That’s part of why I came in, really. For months now it’s been all turned around. Some days I barely eat anything that feels like a real meal — just coffee, maybe toast, and then I keep putting off eating properly. And then other days I’ll be standing in the bakery aisle buying cookies or pastries, like some part of me thinks that will settle something down.

But then I get home and I don’t even really enjoy them. I’ll eat some or just look at them and feel foolish, like, why did I do that? So yes, I think it does connect to feeling emotionally out of control, but not in a planned way. It feels more like my eating gets pulled along by whatever is happening inside me.
Are your eating habits affecting your relationships with family or friends?

A little, yes… not like there’s been some big argument about it, but I think it affects how I am around people. Meals are social, aren’t they? And when my eating is so turned around, it makes me awkward about seeing people.

Like, if someone asks if I want to come over or go out for something to eat, I feel this pressure because I don’t know what kind of day it’s going to be. Some days I’m barely picking at toast and drinking coffee, and I don’t want anyone watching me not eat. Then other days I’ve been in the bakery aisle buying sweets, cookies or pastries, and I don’t even really enjoy them when I get them home, so I feel embarrassed and sort of ashamed about that too.

So I suppose I pull back a bit. I don’t want family or friends making comments, even kind comments, because then I have to explain something I don’t really understand myself. It’s one of the reasons I came in, honestly. It’s been going on for months, and it’s started to feel like it’s not just about food anymore — it gets in the way of feeling normal around people.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill your responsibilities as a caregiver for your aunt due to your current eating habits?

Yes… I mean, I still do the basic things for my aunt. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve just stopped caring for her, because I haven’t. I still make sure the necessary things get done, the things that really can’t be skipped.

But it has gotten harder than it used to be. My eating being so irregular sort of throws off the whole day, and then I don’t have the same steadiness I used to have. I’ve missed some church planning calls, which I normally would have kept up with, and I’ve put off things for the fair that I said I would help with. Those are the kinds of things I used to just handle without thinking very much about it.

And lately I’ve had to ask neighbors to cover things here and there, things I used to manage myself. That makes me feel bad, because I don’t like feeling unreliable, especially when my aunt depends on me and when people in town are used to me being involved. So yes, I’m getting through the basics, but everything around it feels much harder than before.
Do you think your eating habits are influenced by a fear of gaining weight?

I don’t think it’s really about being afraid of gaining weight, no. At least, that’s not how it feels to me.

It’s more like… my eating has just gotten all turned around, and that’s one of the reasons I came in. For months now, some days I’ll barely manage anything that feels like food — just picking at toast, drinking coffee, putting off a proper meal like I can’t quite get myself to do it. And then other days I’ll find myself standing in the bakery aisle buying sweets, cookies or pastries, almost like I’m on autopilot.

But it’s not because I’m thinking about my weight, exactly. I don’t even really enjoy the sweets once I get them home half the time. I just sit there with them and feel strange about it, like I don’t understand why I bought them. So no, I wouldn’t say fear of gaining weight is what’s driving it. It feels more confused than that.
Do you usually buy or eat sweets when you are feeling sad or empty?

Yes… I think so, at least some of the time. It’s hard to say it neatly, because it doesn’t feel like, “Oh, I’m sad, so now I’ll have a cookie,” in a normal sort of way. It’s more like I’ll be feeling low or hollow, and then later I realize I’m standing in the bakery aisle buying sweets or pastries, even though I don’t especially want them.

And that’s part of why I came in, really. My eating has been all turned around for months now. Some days I’m just picking at toast and drinking coffee, like a proper meal is too much to manage. Then other days I end up buying cookies or sweets, and when I get them home, I don’t even enjoy them much. I just sort of sit there with them and feel embarrassed, or confused about why I did it.

So yes, I suppose when I’m feeling empty, it can happen. But it doesn’t feel comforting exactly. It feels more automatic than comforting.
Are you finding it difficult to manage your daily tasks and responsibilities due to your current eating habits?

Yes… yes, I am, though I keep wanting to explain that I’m still doing the things that absolutely have to be done. I still make sure my aunt is cared for in the basic ways, and I don’t want anyone thinking I’ve just let everything go, because I haven’t.

But it’s harder now. The way I’m eating, or not eating, it throws off my energy and my timing, and then the day sort of gets away from me. I’ve missed church planning calls I normally would have been on top of, and I’ve put off some of the fair projects I said I’d help with. Those kinds of things used to feel manageable, just part of what I did.

Lately I’ve also had to ask neighbors to cover little things I used to handle myself, and that bothers me a lot. I don’t like feeling like people can’t count on me. So I’m getting through the basics, but caregiving and staying involved in town feel much harder than they used to.
Are your eating habits causing you significant distress or impairment in your daily life?

Yes… it is. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely unable to function, because I do still get through the basics, especially for my aunt. I make sure the necessary things happen. I’m still trying very hard not to let her down.

But it’s definitely causing problems. When I’m not eating properly, or when my eating is all over the place, I just don’t have the steadiness I used to have. I’ve missed church planning calls that I normally would have remembered and been prepared for. I’ve put off fair projects I said I would help with, and that weighs on me because people are counting on me.

And I’ve had to ask neighbors to cover little things I used to handle without even thinking about it. That part is embarrassing, honestly. It makes me feel like I’m slipping in ways other people might notice. So yes, it’s distressing, and it’s made caregiving and staying involved in town feel much harder than it used to.
